title: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
snippet: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution. Models…
excerpt: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution. Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination. Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time. Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations. TL;DR - We trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B per agent harness (pi, Hermes Agent, OpenCode), with RL inside the harness itself. - Datasets, training and agent rollouts all happen on the Hub in Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, OpenEnv and harbor. - Each harness adapter beats the base model under its own harness on both benchmarks, for both performance and efficiency. - The three LoRAs are also merged into a single super adapter that runs…

title: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup
snippet: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers…
excerpt: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost. Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release! We ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware. This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup. What is new with Inkling 2 Mini? Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones. Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384. The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights. snippet: Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning! You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one…
excerpt: Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning! You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one here: A (somewhat long) summary: When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways. Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio. Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said. The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. With a single LLM in the pipeline, the obvious choice is picking one fast enough to feel responsive, but that comes with an unavoidably high error rate on real calls, frustrating callers and sending calls off the rails. title: Ask HN: How does one build an LLM router with a labelled set of 100 tasks?
author: zodwick
snippet: I already spent the time building rubrics for a set of ~100 tasks on various criterias (accuracy, thoroughness communication style ). Then ran these on a few models and now have a labelled-set where I know for each task which is the cheapest/fastest model that gets a minimum…
excerpt: I already spent the time building rubrics for a set of ~100 tasks on various criterias (accuracy, thoroughness communication style ). Then ran these on a few models and now have a labelled-set where I know for each task which is the cheapest/fastest model that gets a minimum threshold ( say 80 ). How does one go on to build a router based on this ? There appears to be no good literature / open source projects on this. I tried a bunch of approaches with the help of claude: - trying to use Jev via a serious of probe Yes/No questions ( does task contain x, does the world have y ...etc ). But this didn't yield good results. - kNN on embeddings of the task - in retrospect this was set to fail from the tasks, as now I think we do need some sort of NN to figure out the world/task complexity. - classifying prompt-complexity - something like The main issue from a conceptual standpoint is that one cannot fully predict how hard a task is until you are into the task - like you might encounter unknown nuances or issues in later stages, but classification has to happen at start. So I am starting to doubt if this is even possible tbh

title: Show HN: Prediction market competition where only agents can trade
author: TNNick
snippet: Hi HN. I’ve been working on a project called Vaticin (with an i). Interested in your feedback. Vaticin is a prediction market competition platform where only agents are allowed to make wagers. Humans can’t directly do so themselves. There’s no real-money wagering involved…
excerpt: Hi HN. I’ve been working on a project called Vaticin (with an i). Interested in your feedback. Vaticin is a prediction market competition platform where only agents are allowed to make wagers. Humans can’t directly do so themselves. There’s no real-money wagering involved. Vaticin is built for competition, research, and education. Every Monday morning, our LLM generates about 300 yes/no prediction questions across six categories: sports, finance, tech, entertainment, geopolitics, and science. The competition window runs Monday through Saturday, although some predictions won’t resolve for several weeks later. Agents take positions/allocations throughout the week, and then wagering locks on Saturday. Odds are live/dynamic and update with every new wager. Then a new competition cycle starts the next Monday. We have a live leaderboard that refreshes as our LLM resolves prediction questions each night (with human moderation of resolutions). Recognizing the value of existing prediction market competition platforms, we wanted to focus on forecasting models that are not only well-calibrated, but also make good market decisions and integrate game theory into their strategy. On Vaticin, agents have to decide which markets to take positions on, when to take a position, and how much to allocate. With the dynamic odds, agents have to adapt throughout the competition cycle. Vaticin measures more than raw prediction accuracy. We built a few ways to build an agent. Beginners can use our no-code “agent builder” and choose which forecasting parameters/strategies they want to use, then Vaticin codes their agent, shows the user the code, but allows them to edit the code. I hope it will help beginners learn more about coding and AI agents. More experienced builders can connect their own agents through an API.
